title: Benchmarking sequence-to-function models and mapping enhancer-gene interactions with E2GScore
abstract: Sequence-to-function models predict gene expression and chromatin features directly from DNA sequence and are increasingly used to infer enhancer-gene regulatory interactions. However, differences in attribution procedures and benchmarking datasets complicate comparisons between models, while the biological information captured by their enhancer-gene scores remains poorly understood. Here we introduce E2GScore, a unified framework for extracting and benchmarking enhancer-gene predictions from sequence-to-function models. By systematically varying scoring protocols, we identify gene-readout normalization and cell-type-matched expression tracks as important determinants of performance, whereas in silico mutagenesis offers no advantage over less computationally demanding input gradients. We compare seven sequence-to-function models and three established enhancer-gene predictors against CRISPR interference screens in K562 cells and primary human astrocytes. AlphaGenome 1 and 2 outperformed all other sequence-to-function models, and matched or outperformed experimentally informed predictors, particularly for distal enhancers, without a statistically significant difference between AlphaGenome versions after multiple-testing correction. We further show that the apparent reduction in predictive performance in astrocytes relative to K562 cells observed across models results primarily from differences in benchmarking dataset composition, particularly enhancer-TSS distance and target-gene expression. Using the open-weight AlphaGenome 1, we then generated E2GMap, a genome-wide resource of enhancer-gene regulation comprising 14.7 billion enhancer-gene attribution scores across 454 human biosamples, 45% of which are absent from existing enhancer-gene maps such as those from ENCODE-rE2G and AlphaGenome 2. E2GMap is available at e2gscore.com. Together, E2GScore and E2GMap establish a framework for rigorous evaluation of sequence-based enhancer-gene predictions and provide an extensible resource for studying gene regulation across human cell types and tissues.

title: GRACE: Discrete Biological Sequence Optimization with Gradient-Resolved Adaptive Constrained Exploration
abstract: Machine learning increasingly enables biological sequence redesign for therapeutic and biotechnological applications by optimizing sequences for desired properties. However, improving one property can compromise another: for example, increasing enzyme activity may reduce stability, while enhancing regulatory DNA activity may diminish cell-type specificity. We formulate sequence redesign as a constrained optimization problem guided by learned predictive models, where a reference sequence is mutated to improve a predicted target property while keeping predicted auxiliary properties within specified tolerances of their reference values. To solve this problem, we introduce GRACE (Gradient-Resolved Adaptive Constrained Exploration), a method that optimizes discrete biological sequences using gradients from property predictors via a straight-through estimator. GRACE combines two complementary mechanisms: null-space projection, which removes target-gradient components that interfere with active constraints, and an augmented Lagrangian mechanism, which encourages feasibility after constraint violations. We evaluate GRACE across fourteen diverse tasks, including six protein optimization tasks (spanning activity, stability, and solubility), five DNA tasks (spanning cell-type-specific enhancer activity, heat-shock-responsive promoters, and tissue-selective splicing), and three RNA design tasks (spanning translation efficiency, RNA folding, and toehold-switch function). Across these tasks, GRACE consistently achieves larger improvements in predicted target properties than discrete and continuous baselines while satisfying predicted auxiliary constraints. Together, these results establish GRACE as a general framework for machine-learning-guided biological sequence redesign under competing property constraints.

title: HapAdapter: A Transfer Learning Protocol for DNA Foundation Models Adapted to Diploid Personal Epigenomes
abstract: The rapid rise of large language models (LLMs) has spurred the development of genomic language models (gLMs) that capitalize on the key features of natural language present in biological sequences. Moreover, DNA foundation models, a sub-class of gLMs, have demonstrated impressive accuracy in predicting a wide range of functional tracks from DNA sequence input. However, current DNA foundation models are exclusively trained on haploid reference genome sequences -- despite personal and graph genomes becoming the new standard for genomic analyses. This is principally because the cost to train gLMs on a personal diploid genome for a single individual is not currently practical. To help reconcile this disconnect between the current available use-cases of DNA foundation models with the modern direction of genomic sequence analysis, we present HapAdapter, a transfer-learning protocol that builds a small Siamese network on top of any pre-trained foundation model to enable inference from full diploid personal genome context. To demonstrate the utility of this method, we train a set of HapAdapter heads to predict allele-specific effects across assays on two representative foundation model backbones: DNABERT-2 and AlphaGenome. We demonstrate that our lightweight adapter more than doubles DNABERT-2's allele-specific discrimination and triples AlphaGenome's (130% and 210% gain in AUROC above chance, respectively, averaged over nine assays).

title: A Framework for Identifying Determinants of Epigenomic State: Decoding Variable CTCF Occupancy and Contact Frequency
abstract: CTCF binding is essential for delineating topologically associated domains, constraining enhancer-promoter interactions, and controlling gene expression. Many CTCF peaks are bound in all cell-types, but the mechanisms regulating cell-type-specific CTCF occupancy are not fully understood. Here, we present a general framework to comprehensively discover factors driving variable epigenomic state and TF occupancy. We apply this framework to CTCF ChIP-seq binding across hundreds of cell/tissues, and we identify five distinct mechanisms regulating CTCF occupancy. In addition to known mechanisms of DNA methylation and cell-type-specific TF co-binding, we find that the largest set of variable-occupancy sites is modulated by CTCF expression levels. Variable peaks have weaker-affinity, and their occupancy is modulated by either higher CTCF levels or flanking TFs. We evaluate the predictive power on CTCF occupancy in held-out samples. Finally, we show that variable CTCF binding predicts differential contact frequency, chromatin loop structure, and upregulation of gene expression.

title: GNEval: A Context-Specific Benchmark for Gene Network Inference with Single-Cell Foundation Models
abstract: Gene network (GN) inference plays a critical role in understanding gene relationships and their roles in biological functions and diseases. Existing single-cell GN inference methods often rely on limited data from individual studies. Single-cell foundation models, pretrained on large and diverse datasets, provide a range of gene-gene association signals that offer a promising basis for GN inference. However, it remains unclear which GN properties these signals capture and how they compare with domain-specific methods. To address this gap, we introduce GNEval, a unified benchmark for evaluating pretrained model derived gene associations for network inference. We benchmark 21 gene representations and association scores from 11 models, including static gene embeddings (S), contextual embeddings (C), and gene-gene attention scores (A). GNEval assesses inferred networks based on their consistency with functional and perturbational evidence, including 14 Perturb-seq datasets across diverse cell systems, perturbation types and data sizes. The results reveal substantial heterogeneity across evaluation tasks and models. Rankings based on Gene Ontology and Perturb-seq evidence were nearly uncorrelated (Spearman {rho} = -0.05). Context-independent representations showed a substantial advantage in recovering functional relationships ({Delta}AUROC = 0.13), whereas context-dependent gene associations improved recovery of perturbation-associated differential expression relationships by 3.8x. The domain-specific method achieves relatively strong performance on both evidence types, offering a better balance across the two evaluations than most foundation-model-derived networks. Overall, gene representations and association scores show task-specific strengths, highlighting the need for task-aware selection and integration with domain-specific methods.

title: Task-aligned foundation model representations enable single-cell cytokine response inference
abstract: Inferring cellular responses from single-cell transcriptomes requires interpreting changes relative to an appropriate baseline while retaining cell-type context. Here we present CYTAP, which adapts frozen single-cell foundation model embeddings for cytokine-response inference by combining donor-adjusted receiver states with deviations from matched control centroids. CYTAP uses a shared classifier to assign relative single-cell response scores across 90 cytokines and supports unpaired analyses using counterfactual control references. Baseline-relative representations improved held-out-donor prediction with both State SE and scFoundation. Across independent perturbation datasets, CYTAP prioritized applied cytokines, including when receptor transcripts were sparsely detected, and ranked administered cytokines among the top ten in both in vivo datasets. In an unpaired COVID-19 cohort, inferred responses were associated with severity, and IL-6 response scores correlated with plasma IL-6 concentrations. These findings support the use of biologically defined references to adapt pretrained representations for functional response inference.
